claim: Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (ICML 2020, dual mirror descent, analytic; horizon T known, requests i.i.d. from an unknown distribution, no refill of a consumed resource inside the horizon): the rule keeps one price per resource, targets a constant consumption per period so as to deplete resources exactly at the end, raises a price when a request uses more than the target and lowers it when less, and never depletes resources too early (Proposition 2).
note: Fetched 2026-11-19. The early-stop gap of Proposition 2 is garbled in the text; with the step size of Theorem 1 it is of order sqrt T rounds (refuter's reading), so not small at T of tens.

claim: Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (ICML 2020, analytic): when horizon and budget grow together the rule's regret is O(sqrt T) and no algorithm does better in order; Theorem 1's bound holds for every T >= 1, but its constants (bounds on revenue and consumption, rho_min, the step size, and the number of resources m to the power 1/2 or 3/2, called sub-optimal by the authors) are garbled in the text, so no number at T of tens was read.

Gaitonde, Li, Light, Lucier and Slivkins (arXiv 2205.08674v6, analytic): gradient pacing sets the target spend rate rho = B/T, bids value/(1 + mu) capped by the remaining budget, moves mu each round by eps x (spend - rho) inside [0, cap], and runs out of budget at most a fixed number of rounds early provided cap >= vmax/rho - 1, eps x vmax <= 1 and no payment exceeds the bid.
note: The gap, read as cap/(eps rho) + vmax/rho rounds, is garbled in the text; at tens of rounds with one unit costing several rounds' budget it can be a large share of the horizon (refuter's reasoning). Clipped at 0, the multiplier does not carry a lull's saving forward (A69).

claim: Chen et al. (arXiv 2207.04690v7, analytic, repeated second-price auctions, horizon known, competing prices i.i.d.): for stochastic values pacing (shading the bid) is generally better than throttling (skipping a share of rounds), and for adversarial values throttling is also asymptotically optimal.

Xu et al. (Yahoo smart pacing, KDD 2015, self-reported; 24-hour budgets, 15-minute slots, tens of billions of ad requests a day): the system re-plans every slot, spreading the remaining budget over the remaining slots.

Xu et al. (Yahoo smart pacing, KDD 2015, self-reported A/B test, 3 campaigns, 24 h, 15-minute slots): pacing in 8 layers by predicted response rate cut cost per click 72, 67 and 79 % against the same system with one global pacing rate, with spending as smooth; no variance is reported.
note: Both arms ran the same pacing loop, so the gain belongs to the value layers; Yahoo chose throttling over bid changes for three reasons, the third being that it decouples pacing from the bid (A13).

claim: Agarwal, Ghosh, Wei and You (LinkedIn, KDD 2014, self-reported, tens of millions of page views a day): each daily budget follows a plan proportional to forecast traffic, and about every minute the participation rate is multiplied by 1.1 when spend to date is at or under the plan and by 0.9 when above; an earlier rule on spent over budget raised revenue but not campaign life, being slow to react.

Agarwal et al. (LinkedIn, KDD 2014, self-reported): 'fast finish' plans each daily budget as if there were no traffic in the last two hours, so that campaigns wrongly throttled earlier get more chance to spend their budget; no effect of it alone is measured.

Agarwal et al. (LinkedIn, KDD 2014, self-reported, pacing on against off on alternate days over two weeks): median campaign life (time to spend 95 % of the daily budget) rose from 13.54 to 19.50 h (+44 %) in Direct Ads, where demand exceeds supply, and from 6.92 to 17.25 h (+149 %) in Sponsored Updates; unique impressions per spend rose 7.74 % and 10.52 %, and over-delivery fell from 3.8 to 3.4 % and from 4.12 to 2.39 %.

Agarwal et al. (LinkedIn, KDD 2014, self-reported): spend is counted with a small delay, so fast-spending campaigns were served after their daily budget was spent; pacing slowed them and cut over-delivery.

Gallego and van Ryzin (1994, analytic; one product, Poisson demand with known intensity, known deadline and stock): one fixed price is asymptotically optimal and earns at least 1 - 1/(2 sqrt(min{n, lambda* t})) of the best dynamic policy, so at least 97.5 % at 400 items, 95 % at 100 and 90 % at 25 when there is time to sell every item at the run-out price; this holds only when the demand function is known in advance and each instance is priced on its own.

Gallego and van Ryzin (1994, numerical example, exponential demand, expected sales 10 at the revenue-maximising price): with 1 to 20 items the best fixed price earned at least 94.5 % of the dynamic optimum and the plain fixed price at least 87.1 % (at 1 item); the authors call the theorem's guarantees quite pessimistic and find dynamic pricing adds about one percent for moderate problems.

Talluri and van Ryzin (1998, network revenue management, analytic): under bid-price control a request that uses several resources is accepted only if capacity is available and its fare exceeds the sum of the bid prices of all the resources it uses.

Talluri and van Ryzin (1998, analytic): summed bid prices are not optimal in general but are asymptotically optimal when capacities and sales volumes grow large, with the right prices constant over time; the sum equals the true opportunity cost only when that cost equals the sum of the costs of selling each resource separately, and in practice the approximation is re-solved often.
note: The paper adds that bid prices fail in part when one sale is a large change in a resource's capacity, which fits a few large units (refuter on A23).

claim: Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins (bandits with knapsacks, analytic, i.i.d. outcomes per arm): with several budgets and time counted as one of them, the process stops when any budget is spent, and choosing arms with one learned price per budget gives regret O(sqrt(m OPT) + OPT sqrt(m/B)), m the number of arms and B the smallest budget, optimal up to log factors.
note: Prices are learned by multiplicative weights; an arm's reward and use are learned, not seen before the choice; with B of tens of units the second term is not small (reasoned).

claim: Devanur, Jain, Sivan and Wilkens (arXiv 1903.03944, analytic, i.i.d. requests): knowing only the number of requests and not their distribution, a price-per-budget rule earns 1 - O(eps) of the offline optimum with probability 1 - delta when no request takes more than gamma = O(eps^2/log(n/delta)) of any capacity or of the optimum, and the trade-off cannot be improved much even with the distribution known.
note: At tens of requests per budget (gamma about 1/30 or more) eps is not small (refuter's reasoning).

claim: Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (WINE 2008 report version, analytic, online knapsack, adversarial order, no clock): taking an item only if its value per weight is at least (Ue/L)^z (L/e), z the share of the budget filled, is (ln(U/L) + 1)-competitive and no online algorithm does better, worsening by the factor 1/(1 - eps0) when the largest item is a share eps0 of the budget; it needs every item small and value per weight between known bounds L and U.
note: Only an archived copy, truncated in section 6. At U/L = 10 and eps0 = 0.05 the guarantee is about 29 % of the offline optimum (refuter's arithmetic, A78).

claim: RFC 2698 (two-rate three-colour marker, IETF 1999, a specification with no measured gain): a packet is green only if both the peak and the committed bucket cover its size, and then both buckets are charged.

ATM Forum Traffic Management 4.0 (1996, a specification with no measured gain): under several rate contracts at once a cell conforms only if it conforms to every one, and each contract's state is updated only by cells that conform.
note: Read from an Internet Archive copy; ITU-T I.371 itself is behind purchase.

claim: Stripe engineering blog (2017, self-reported, no before-and-after figure): a fixed share of capacity is always reserved for critical requests (20 % in the example), and non-critical requests above their 80 % are rejected with status 503.

Google SRE book chapter 21 (self-reported, no baseline figure): client-side throttling lets a client send until its requests are K times its accepts, K = 2 preferred, and allows retries while they are under 10 % of requests, with at most three attempts per request.

Google SRE book chapter 22 (self-reported, qualitative): retries multiply across layers, so that one user action may create 64 attempts (4^3), and a server-wide retry budget is advised (the example allows 60 retries per minute in a process).

Anthropic engineering post on its multi-agent research system (13 June 2025, self-reported): on BrowseComp token usage alone explained 80 % of the variance in performance, upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 gained more than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7, and multi-agent systems used about 15 times the tokens of chats; the post says most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelisable parts than research.

Tsafrir (2006 PhD thesis, chapter 4, Table 4.3; simulation replaying four real logs, CTC, KTH, SDSC and BLUE, 100 to 1,152 processors, 28,490 to 223,407 jobs over 11 to 32 months, load 56 to 84 %, mean run 73 to 188 min): EASY++ (system-predicted lengths corrected when outlived, backfill candidates shortest first) cut average wait 23 % and bounded slowdown 37 % against EASY with user estimates; shortest-first backfilling alone gave 10 % and 22 %, exact lengths (PERFECT++) 22 % and 47 %.
note: On SDSC the wait gain of EASY++ was 10 %. A job takes many processors, so the processor count overstates how many jobs ran at once.

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis, Table 4.1, the same four logs): replacing user estimates by system predictions without correction raised accuracy 49 % on average but made wait 454 % and bounded slowdown 515 % worse on average (per log +38 to +920 %), because under-predicted running jobs move the reservation to the present and stop backfilling.

Tsafrir (2006 thesis): doubling users' length estimates (all too long, less accurate) tends to help backfilling, with real and with perfect estimates, but EASY++ beats doubling by a wide margin on all traces and both metrics and comes close to shortest-job-first.

Tsafrir (2006 thesis): the length predictor is the mean of the same user's two most recent finished jobs; using more history made results worse, though two jobs are slightly better than one, and when a job outlives its prediction it is best to raise the prediction straight to the user's full estimate.
note: The last two parts were added by the refuter (paper.txt 4711-4714, 4774) and found at those lines by the fold step, not by the gate.

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis, citing another study not read in its own text): average utilisation on five supercomputers over eleven years went from 40-60 % to about 70 % once backfilling was introduced, a before-and-after observation and not a controlled comparison, and backfilling was a close second to schemes with preemption, migration and dynamic partitioning.

Tsafrir (2006 thesis): EASY backfilling requires a runtime estimate for every job and kills a job that exceeds its estimate, so as not to violate the reservation; the reservation order stays first come, first served and only backfill candidates are taken shortest first.
note: The order sentence is at paper.txt 4120-4122, cited by the refuter and found there by the fold step.

claim: Lifka (JSSPP 1995, ANL/IBM SP scheduler, no measured figure): backfilling starts a job further down the queue on idle nodes only if it does not make the first job in the queue wait any longer.

Kolisch and Hartmann (EJOR 2006; deterministic durations and demands, one project): at 1,000 / 5,000 / 50,000 schedules the best methods are 0.10 / 0.04 / 0.00 % above the optimum at 30 activities (Kochetov and Stolyar), 11.73 / 11.10 / 10.71 % above the critical-path lower bound at 60 activities (Debels et al.), and 34.07 / 32.54 / 31.24 % above that bound at 120 activities (Valls et al.), over 480, 480 and 600 instances.
note: a1-collect-longjobs.md lines 10 and 47 label the 11.73 / 11.10 / 10.71 row as 120 activities; the table captions put it in the 60-activity table. The 60- and 120-activity gaps are to a lower bound, so they overstate the gap to the optimum by an unknown amount.

claim: Dean and Ghemawat (MapReduce, OSDI 2004, self-reported, one sort on about 1,800 machines): backup copies of the last running tasks typically add no more than a few percent of resources, and the sort took 44 % longer with them disabled.

Zaharia et al. (LATE, OSDI 2008; EC2 virtual machines, 30 GB sort with 486 map and 437 reduce tasks per job, 6 runs): speculatively running the task estimated to finish farthest in the future, from a constant progress rate, capped at 10 % of task slots, finished jobs 27 % faster on average than Hadoop's native speculation, and 58 % faster in a setup with induced stragglers (25 GB, 4 experiments).
note: The 27 % is a mean over runs with high variance; one copy is a small share of a job of hundreds of tasks.

claim: Ananthanarayanan et al. (Mantri, OSDI 2010, Bing production cluster, self-reported): Mantri does not restart a task that runs long because it has more work, and job completion was 32 % shorter in June runs than in April-May runs of the same jobs on the earlier build, a before-and-after comparison.

Ananthanarayanan et al. (Dolly, NSDI 2013; Hadoop prototype on 150 nodes replaying Facebook and Bing traces, heavy-tailed job sizes): cloning every task of small jobs from the start, within a 5 % resource budget, cut small jobs' average completion time 34 % against LATE and 46 % against Mantri.

evidence: docs/program/evidence/round3-2026-11-18/a1-report.md#(a) The rule for spending a refilling allowance

claim: proposed correction of o2-0501: papers read do pace a budget over a known horizon (Balseiro-Lu-Mirrokni, Gaitonde et al.), Yahoo and LinkedIn paced 24-hour budgets in production (self-reported), and bandits with knapsacks treats several budgets at once; no source models a refill inside a horizon, so a window that resets is one horizon and the next window a new one (reasoned); the window semantics are documented, not to be measured (the five-hour period starts at the first message and resets in full five hours later, the weekly reset is at a fixed time per account); still open are two windows counting the same tokens, carry-over, cache weight in Claude Code and the sizes.

proposed correction of o2-0404: 'no paper bounds a window of hours or days' does not hold, since the bounds read are stated per number of decisions for a horizon of any clock length (Balseiro-Lu-Mirrokni's Theorem 1 for any T >= 1 with constants unread, Gallego-van Ryzin at 1 to 400 items for known demand, Zhou et al. in the worst case at any scale) and LinkedIn measured daily budgets (self-reported); its other part stands, since whether an unspent part is lost at a reset is still not documented.

proposed correction of o2-0317 (its note only): 'no paper read bounds a window of hours or days' does not hold, since pacing and fixed-stock bounds are stated per number of decisions for a horizon of any clock length (Balseiro-Lu-Mirrokni, Gallego-van Ryzin, Zhou et al.); the result itself (Parekh and Gallager) is not questioned.

proposed correction of r57-0408: the token allowance limits starts not only when a window is nearly spent; under both the re-planning form and the price form, when demand exceeds the window it limits starts from the moment spend runs ahead of the window's time share (u > s), and LinkedIn found a rule on spent over budget alone slow to react.

proposed correction of r57-0409: the token allowance as one more width is covered in part by papers read, since a unit must fit in every bucket (RFC 2698, ATM Forum TM 4.0) and is priced at the sum of the prices of the budgets it uses (Talluri and van Ryzin, bandits with knapsacks); only the assembly for our windows is reasoning, and its age cap has a published alternative, a reservation for the oldest waiting unit (Lifka, Tsafrir).

proposed correction of o2-0321: RouteLLM's 3.66 times is fewer GPT-4 calls than random routing, not than all-GPT-4, to recover half the quality gap on MT Bench, where that is 95 % of GPT-4's quality; the MMLU 1.41 and GSM8K 1.49 are at 92 % and 87 %.

proposed correction of o2-0320: with the large quality gap the three routers lost 13.8, 13.1 and 10.3 % quality at 40 % routed to the small model, and only the transformed router beat random; the record gives only the best router's 10.3 %.

proposed correction of x19-0701: the do_not reason it points at, that speculative backup tasks double token cost, does not hold as the literature does it (MapReduce, LATE and Dolly copy only the tail, within a few percent to 10 % of capacity); for model sessions a copy does pay a whole unit's tokens, so a copy is justified only when the time saved is worth the summed window price times its tokens and the unit is slow from the run, not from more work.
